newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Berl sees NZ 90-day rate at 6.0 pct by early 1998.
newsitem.headline: Berl sees NZ 90-day rate at 6.0 pct by early 1998.

text.p: Economic forecaster BERL said on Monday it expected New Zealand's 90-day bank bill rate to move to a new low of 6.0 percent by early next year.

BERL chief executive, Kel Sanderson, said business people would be thinking they were living with Alice in Wonderland, given the recent rise in New Zealand mortgage rates to 10.4 percent from 8.95 percent in a troughing economy.

"The increase in mortgage rates defies logic in terms of the economy which actually contracted in the March quarter this year, and going by the slack retail sales and job losses in most industries in the June quarter, is probably still contracting,"
"The lift in interest rates is a knee-jerk reaction by the banks to a temporary rise in the 90-day bank bill rate as part of the interplay between interest rates and the exchange rate.
"The 90-day rate is forecast to move down to a new low of 6.0 percent by early next year," Sanderson added.

He said the muddled tug-of-war between the banks, the finance sector and the economy managers, especially the Reserve Bank, was forecast to result in a further depreciation of the currency to a Trade-Weighted Index of 60 to 62 by the end of the year.
BERL said the return of the exchange rate to lower levels will sustain a growing economy in future, and will not result in high inflation.

The size of the overall economy, measured by GDP, increased by just 1.8 percent in calendar 1996, and BERL forecast a further slowdown over the next few months, then some recovery to finish with an increase of 1.4 percent in the year to March 1998.

"Thereafter the steady recovery should get underway, and GDP grow by 2.0 percent in the year to March 1999, and then a healthy, sustainable, non-inflationary 4.0 percent to usher in the new millennium to March 2000," BERL said.
But it forecast the government surplus on the Adjusted Financial Balance to drop to about NZ$650 million in the year to June 1998 from $2.1 billion in the year to June 1997.

The surplus was forecast to drop down to a zero balance or even a budget deficit of up to $150 million in the year to June 1999, and then return to a surplus the following year with emerging business growth lifting tax revenues.

BERL forecast the current account deficit to blow out to $5.4 billion in the year to June 2000 from about $4 billion in 1996-97, which it said would seriously damage New Zealand's stading with international investors.
